findings.title: Migration fixtures are always well-formed, so a throwing migration that permanently hangs boot is green
findings.description:
`seedLegacyLocalStorage()` is the only fixture in the file and it writes syntactically perfect, correctly-shaped JSON every time: a real array of book objects, a real profile object, and `pdfData: btoa('fake pdf bytes')` (valid base64). No test writes valid JSON of the WRONG type, and no test writes a `pdfData` value that isn't base64. Both are unhandled in production and both brick the app permanently.

Production path: `migrate.ts:54-62` does `JSON.parse(raw) as T` inside a try/catch that only catches SYNTAX errors — a stored `{}` or `5` parses fine and is then asserted to be `LegacyBook[]`. `migrate.ts:99` does `readJson<LegacyBook[]>(key) ?? []` (the `??` only rescues `null`), and `migrate.ts:101` immediately does `for (const legacy of legacyBooks)` -> `TypeError: legacyBooks is not iterable`. A stored JSON string instead of an array is worse: `for...of` iterates its CHARACTERS and silently creates one 'Untitled' book per character. Separately, `migrate.ts:118/136` reads `legacy.pdfData`, typed `string | undefined` purely by the `as T` assertion, and hands it to `base64ToBytes` -> `atob`, which throws `InvalidCharacterError` on anything that isn't base64 (a data-URL-prefixed `data:application/pdf;base64,...` value — the obvious shape for the original app to have stored — contains `:`, `;` and `,` and throws).

Why it is critical rather than merely a crash: `MIGRATION_MARKER` is written at `migrate.ts:149`, AFTER the loop. `ProfileContext.tsx:31` awaits `migrateLegacyData()` as the first statement of an un-caught `void (async () => {...})()` boot effect, so a throw (a) leaves `isLoading` permanently `true` — the app never renders past the loading state — (b) surfaces only as an unhandled rejection, bypassing the error boundary, and (c) leaves the marker unwritten so the identical failure repeats on every reload forever. It also leaves partially-written IndexedDB records, so the `is idempotent` test at line 137 (which only ever runs the happy path) guarantees nothing about the failure path — a retry would duplicate books.

What goes untested: every non-happy legacy payload. The suite proves the migration works on data the test itself wrote in the correct shape.

 10     'booksum_db_users',
 ...
 25   localStorage.setItem(
 26     `booksum_library_${LEGACY_USER_ID}`,
 27     JSON.stringify([          // <- always a real array; never `{}`, `5` or a string
 ...
 42         pdfData: btoa('fake pdf bytes'),   // <- always valid base64; never a data: URL

-- migrate.ts --

101     for (const legacy of legacyBooks) {       // throws on {} or 5
149   localStorage.setItem(MIGRATION_MARKER, ...); // marker written LAST

findings.title: apiError fixture defaults its message to 'boom', so the 403 -> invalid-key assertion proves nothing
findings.description:
The `apiError` helper defaults `message` to the literal string `'boom'` — a value that matches NONE of the substring branches in `toAiError`. Every row of the `it.each` table on lines 14-23 therefore reaches the status switch at `errors.ts:57-61` unopposed, and the table passes for a reason unrelated to how real Gemini errors are classified.

`errors.ts:53-61` checks message substrings BEFORE status: `lower.includes('quota')`, then `lower.includes('safety') || lower.includes('blocked')`, and only then falls through to the status codes. Google's HTTP-referrer / API-key-restriction rejection is a 403 whose message is `"Requests from referer <empty> are blocked."` — it contains `blocked`, so it is classified `safety`, not `invalid-key`, and the user is told "Gemini blocked this request under its safety filters. Try a different book or wording." instead of being pointed at their key in Settings. The test at line 17 asserts exactly the opposite behaviour and is green, because `'boom'` dodges the branch.

The deeper type problem this fixture hides: `AiErrorKind` is a discriminated union built by ad-hoc substring matching over an unstructured, unvalidated `message: string` from a third-party SDK. There is no runtime validation of the error shape at all, and the one test file that exists cannot detect precedence bugs because its fixture message is inert. What goes untested: every real Gemini error message, and the entire message-before-status precedence order.

findings.title: Migration test asserts summaryId but never the denormalised oneSentenceTakeaway it must move with
findings.description:
The `splits each legacy book into a Book and a Summary` test asserts `status`, `hasPdf`, `readingTimeMinutes` and `summaryId` on the migrated `Book`, and `keyInsights`/`model` on the `Summary`. It never asserts `atomic?.oneSentenceTakeaway` — even though the legacy fixture supplies it on line 33 (`oneSentenceTakeaway: 'Small changes compound.'`) and the migration reads it on `migrate.ts:125` to build the Summary.

`migrate.ts:105-119` builds the `Book` with `summaryId` set but WITHOUT `oneSentenceTakeaway`. `types.ts:41-50` documents `oneSentenceTakeaway` and `readingTimeMinutes` as deliberately denormalised onto `Book` so list views render without loading summaries, and `BookCard.tsx:89` reads exactly that field: `{book.oneSentenceTakeaway ? `"${book.oneSentenceTakeaway}"` : 'Not summarised yet'}`. So every migrated book renders "Not summarised yet" in the library grid despite having a full summary. The `AddBookModal.tsx:72` path sets it correctly, and `LibraryPage.tsx:92` re-syncs it after a generate — the migration is the one producer that drops it, and the one producer with no assertion covering it.

The type-system root cause: `Book.summaryId?` and `Book.oneSentenceTakeaway?` are two independently-optional fields that must be present or absent together. Nothing in the type makes `{ summaryId: set, oneSentenceTakeaway: undefined }` unrepresentable, so the compiler happily accepted the incomplete `books.create` call. A discriminated union on the summarised state (or a single required `summaryRef?: { id, takeaway }`) would have made this a compile error rather than a silent UI regression.

findings.title: base64 suite has two happy-path tests only; base64ToBytes is total in its type but throws on the one input path it serves
findings.description:
The whole suite is a round-trip of six clean bytes and one decode of a hand-written valid base64 string. Neither test feeds invalid base64, an empty string, a data-URL prefix, or a non-string coerced through `as`.

`base64.ts:5` declares `base64ToBytes(base64: string): Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` — a total function with no error channel in its type. `atob` throws `InvalidCharacterError` (a `DOMException`) for any input containing characters outside the base64 alphabet. The function's ONLY production callers are `migrate.ts:136` and `migrate.ts:142`, which pass `legacy.pdfData` and `legacy.audioData` straight from `JSON.parse` of localStorage — values whose `string | undefined` type comes entirely from the `as T` assertion at `migrate.ts:58` and has never been validated. A legacy record holding `data:application/pdf;base64,JVBERi0...` (the natural way for the pre-IndexedDB app to have stashed a PDF) or a non-string throws here, and per L13-F03 that throw permanently hangs boot.

The migration test's own fixture at `migrate.test.ts:42` uses `btoa('fake pdf bytes')`, so it too can never reach this. Between the two suites, the decoder is proven only against input the tests themselves encoded. What goes untested: every real legacy `pdfData`/`audioData` value.

findings.title: The only books.create fixture cannot produce a fat record, so the 'no binary data in records' invariant is unguarded
findings.description:
`bookInput()` is the sole fixture feeding `books.create` in the storage suite, and its `overrides` parameter is typed `Partial<Parameters<typeof books.create>[0]>` — which structurally forbids the fixture from ever carrying a key that isn't on `Book`. So no test in this file can produce the failure mode the repo is supposed to prevent.

`repo.ts:54-58` does `const book: Book = { ...input, id, addedAt }` and persists it verbatim. TypeScript's excess-property check does not fire on properties introduced by a spread, and does not fire at all when the argument is a variable rather than a fresh literal — which is exactly how `useLibrary.tsx:111` calls it during a library import: `await bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id })`, where `book` comes from `payload.books` of a `LibraryExport` produced by `JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport` at `ProfileView.tsx:117`. That is an unvalidated user-supplied file. Any extra key on it — `pdfData`, `audioData`, a base64 cover — is copied straight into the `books` object store. CLAUDE.md names this as the exact defect that broke the original app ("No binary data in records... This is what broke the original app").

`migrate.test.ts:101` (`expect('pdfData' in (atomic as object)).toBe(false)`) is the only runtime guard for the invariant anywhere in the lot, and it covers the migration path only — not the import path, which is the one with an untrusted producer. What goes untested: `books.create` / `books.update` with any object carrying keys outside `Book`.

findings.title: mockFetch types every API fixture as unknown, so no fixture is checked against the as-asserted response shapes
findings.description:
`mockFetch(handler: (url: string) => unknown)` returns `unknown`, so every response fixture in this file — `{ items: [{ volumeInfo: { imageLinks: { large } } }] }` on line 24, `{ docs: [{ cover_i: 12345 }] }` on line 36 — is invisible to the compiler. Those two assertions at `googleBooks.ts:12-14` and `openLibrary.ts:6` are the ONLY types the app has for two external HTTP APIs, and the tests that are supposed to pin them cannot detect drift between fixture and assertion in either direction.

Concrete gaps this creates:
- `googleBooks.ts:13` types `imageLinks?: Record<string, string>`. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (measured baseline), `links.extraLarge` is typed `string` — non-optional — while at runtime it is `undefined` for the vast majority of Google Books volumes, which return only `thumbnail`/`smallThumbnail`. The `??` chain on lines 19-23 works by accident of runtime `undefined`, not because the type says so. No fixture exercises an `imageLinks` object missing `large`, so the fallback ladder below line 20 is never executed by any test.
- No fixture produces a 200 with a non-JSON body, even though `mockFetch` can: a handler returning `undefined` makes `JSON.stringify(result)` evaluate to `undefined`, yielding a 200 with an empty body, and `response.json()` then throws `SyntaxError` — swallowed silently by the bare `catch {}` at `index.ts:17`, which would degrade every cover to a placeholder with no signal.
- No fixture exercises `items: [{}]` (an entry with no `volumeInfo`) or `docs: [{}]` (no `cover_i`).

What goes untested: the whole malformed/partial-response half of two `as`-asserted boundaries, plus the `Record<string, string>` claim that every key is a present string.

findings.title: src/lib/ai ships 11 modules and 2 test files; every JSON.parse-as-T boundary is in the untested nine
findings.description:
`src/lib/ai` contains `apiKey.ts`, `chat.ts`, `client.ts`, `errors.ts`, `models.ts`, `prompts.ts`, `quiz.ts`, `recommend.ts`, `schemas.ts`, `summarize.ts`, `tts.ts`. Exactly two test files exist: `apiKey.test.ts` (which also covers `client.ts` via `getClient`) and `errors.test.ts`. Everything that actually parses a model response is untested.

All four `JSON.parse(...) as T` sites live in that untested set and none has a runtime guard:
- `summarize.ts:52` and `summarize.ts:73` — `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as RawBookResponse`
- `recommend.ts:30` — `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { ... }`
- `quiz.ts:16` — `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { questions?: QuizQuestion[] }`

The `responseSchema` passed to Gemini is a request hint, not a validator, and the coalescing in `summarize.ts:28-37` (`data.rating ?? 0`, `data.keyInsights ?? []`) only rescues `null`/`undefined` — it cannot rescue a wrong TYPE. A model returning `keyInsights: "Systems beat goals"` or `rating: "5"` produces a `Summary`/`Book` whose declared field types are lies, which are then written to IndexedDB and become permanently wrong records. `quiz.ts:17` `return data.questions ?? []` hands `QuizQuestion[]` straight to the SRS card factory with `correctAnswerIndex` unbounded against `options.length`.

This is a risk multiplier rather than a standalone defect: the assertion is the only type, and there is no test to notice when the runtime disagrees. What goes untested: every AI response shape the app ingests.

findings.title: Summary fixture always supplies real arrays, so the one consumer that would crash on an AI-shaped Summary is never exercised
findings.description:
The `summary` fixture is annotated `: Summary`, which is the right pattern and forces field completeness — but every array field is a hand-written real array (`keyInsights: ['Systems beat goals.', 'Identity drives habit.']`, `actionableSteps: ['Habit stack.']`), and the only variation the suite tries is the EMPTY array on line 70. Nothing in the lot ever hands `bookToMarkdown` a `Summary` whose fields came from `JSON.parse(...) as RawBookResponse`.

That matters because `markdown.ts` is the crash site for the untyped AI boundary. `summarize.ts:36` builds `keyInsights: data.keyInsights ?? []` from an unvalidated model response; `??` passes a string straight through. `markdown.ts:24-25` then does `if (summary.keyInsights.length > 0) { ...summary.keyInsights.map((i) => `- ${i}`) }` — a non-empty string satisfies `.length > 0` and then throws `TypeError: summary.keyInsights.map is not a function`, killing the library export. `markdown.ts:27-28` has the identical shape for `actionableSteps`.

So the type says `keyInsights: string[]`, the producer never checks, and the consumer's only tests supply values that make the claim true by construction. What goes untested: `bookToMarkdown`/`libraryToMarkdown` against any `Summary` that came off the wire rather than out of the test file. (The fixture itself is otherwise exemplary — explicitly annotated, complete, and the `Book` fixture on lines 5-18 likewise.)

findings.title: No fixture passes a non-object to toAiError(error: unknown), which throws on null/undefined via an unguarded as-cast
findings.description:
Every fixture in this file constructs a real `Error`: `apiError()` on lines 4-6, `new MissingKeyError()`, `new TypeError(...)`, `new SyntaxError(...)`. Nothing ever passes `null`, `undefined`, a bare string or a number — the values `toAiError(error: unknown)` explicitly declares it accepts.

`errors.ts:39-42` does `const status = (error as { status?: unknown }).status;` with no null guard. For `undefined` the flow is: `message = String(undefined)` -> `'undefined'`, which contains none of `quota`/`safety`/`blocked`; not a `SyntaxError`; not a `TypeError`; so it falls to the `else` on line 57 and dereferences `.status` on `undefined` -> `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'status')`. Same for `null`.

`toAiError` is the app's universal error normaliser — every AI entry point wraps its body in `catch (error) { throw toAiError(error) }` (`summarize.ts:56/77/101`, `quiz.ts:19`, and the rest). A function whose entire job is to turn ANYTHING into a friendly `AiError` instead throws a raw `TypeError` for two of the values its own parameter type admits, so instead of a toast the user gets an unhandled rejection. `Promise.reject()` with no argument and `throw undefined` from third-party code both reach it. The `as { status?: unknown }` is the lie: it claims the value is an object.

What goes untested: the non-object branch of a function typed to accept `unknown`.

findings.title: setup.ts provides no typed fetch stub, so four hand-rolled stubs diverge from typeof fetch and one leaks across tests
findings.description:
`setup.ts` wires jest-dom, fake-indexeddb, an `asyncUtilTimeout` and an `afterEach` cleanup — but no shared browser-API stubbing. Every suite that needs `fetch` hand-rolls its own, and `vi.stubGlobal(name, value: unknown)` accepts anything, so the compiler never checks any of them against `typeof globalThis.fetch`. Four divergent stubs result:
- `smoke.test.tsx:43` — `(input: RequestInfo | URL) => Promise<Response>`, drops the `init` parameter entirely
- `covers/index.test.ts:8` — same, drops `init`
- `covers/index.test.ts:56` — `async () => { throw ... }`, zero parameters, inferred `Promise<never>`
- `covers/index.test.ts:64` — drops `init` again
Dropping `init` means any production `fetch(url, { signal, headers, method })` has its options silently discarded under test, and any assertion written over `call[1]` would be untypeable. Real `fetch` returns `Promise<Response>` and can reject; the `Promise<never>` stub is not assignable to it and nothing says so.

Second, concrete consequence of there being no shared helper: `smoke.test.tsx:61` calls `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` as the last statement of the test BODY rather than in an `afterEach`. `restoreMocks: true` in `vite.config.ts:24` restores spies but does not undo `stubGlobal`, and `unstubGlobals` is not set. If any assertion between lines 49 and 60 fails, the stubbed `fetch` — which answers every request with a fixed 200 `{}` — leaks into the two later tests in the same file, silently changing what they exercise. `covers/index.test.ts:16-18` gets this right with an `afterEach`; nothing enforces the difference.

The fix shape is a single typed helper in `setup.ts` (`stubFetch(fn: typeof globalThis.fetch)`) plus `unstubGlobals: true`, which restores the compiler check and centralises teardown. Also absent: any stub for `URL.createObjectURL`/`revokeObjectURL` (see L13-F10).

findings.title: The 'no Gemini call on boot' invariant is asserted by a for-loop that runs zero times when nothing is captured
findings.description:
`makes no network call to Gemini on boot` guards one of CLAUDE.md's stated invariants, and its entire assertion is a `for` loop over `fetchSpy.mock.calls`. If `mock.calls` is empty the loop body never executes and the test passes having asserted nothing at all. There is no `expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenCalled()`, no `expect.assertions(n)`, and no check that the spy was actually installed in the path under test.

That makes the test indistinguishable between three outcomes: (a) boot genuinely made no request — the intended pass; (b) boot made requests through a `fetch` reference captured at module-import time, before `vi.stubGlobal` ran on line 47, so the spy never saw them; (c) a future refactor moves the network call somewhere the spy does not cover. Only (a) is the invariant; all three are green.

The stub also returns a fixed `new Response('{}', { status: 200 })` for every URL, so even if a Gemini call happened it would be answered successfully rather than surfacing as a failure. The identical pattern is at `covers/index.test.ts:72-74` (`never calls a Gemini endpoint`), where the loop does currently run — but nothing keeps it that way.

What goes untested: whether the spy is on the path at all. The cheap fix is asserting a non-zero call count (or `expect.hasAssertions()`) alongside the URL check.

findings.title: download.test.ts covers only slugify; downloadText has no return annotation and cannot run under the current harness
findings.description:
The module exports two functions. Only `slugify` is tested, and it is tested well (5 cases including the empty-result fallback and the length cap). `downloadText` — the function that actually performs the user-visible export — has zero coverage and cannot be given any without harness work.

`download.ts:2` declares `export function downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')` with no return type annotation, on an exported symbol. More importantly it calls `URL.createObjectURL` (line 4) and `URL.revokeObjectURL` (line 11). jsdom does not implement either, and `src/test/setup.ts` stubs neither, so any test touching this path dies with `TypeError: URL.createObjectURL is not a function`. `lib.dom` declares both as unconditionally present, so the compiler asserts a capability the test environment does not have — the ambient type is a lie about the runtime the suite runs in.

The same gap blocks three other production call sites: `ProfileView.tsx:99` (library JSON export), `BookDetail.tsx:160` (TTS playback) and `:199` (PDF open), and `EReader.tsx:204`. `useTheme.test.tsx:28` demonstrates the pattern for the analogous `matchMedia` gap by stubbing it per-file rather than in `setup.ts`.

What goes untested: the entire download/blob-URL surface, including the `revokeObjectURL` cleanup that prevents leaked object URLs.

findings.title: The cascade test omits reviewCards, and the whole reviewCards store surface is untested
findings.description:
`removes the summary and blobs when a book is removed` asserts three things after `books.remove`: the book is gone, the summary is gone, the blob is gone. It does not assert that review cards are gone, even though `repo.ts:72` calls `reviewCards.removeByBook(id)` in that same cascade and `ReviewCard` rows carry a `bookId` foreign key. The profile-level cascade test on lines 88-97 has the same omission. Nothing in `repo.test.ts` touches `reviewCards` at all — `listByProfile`, `listDue`, `listByBook`, `upsert` and `removeByBook` (repo.ts:77-109) have zero coverage in the module's own suite.

That matters for type honesty because `reviewCards.listByProfile` and `listByBook` are raw `getDb().getAll('reviewCards')` reads typed solely by the `BookSumDB` schema declaration at `db.ts:12-16`. Nothing validates that a stored row is actually a `ReviewCard`; the declaration is an assertion about the contents of a store the app has been writing to since v1. Orphaned cards from a book deleted before the cascade existed would be returned as `ReviewCard[]` and fed to the review UI with a `bookId` that resolves to nothing.

More generally, every read test in this file is a closed loop: the suite writes with `profiles.create`/`books.create`, then reads back with `profiles.list`/`books.listByProfile`. No fixture ever puts a record into the store that the repo did not itself construct, so the schema's type claims can never be falsified. `profiles.list` at `repo.ts:9` does `a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt)` — an unguarded dereference on a field that only the repo's own writer guarantees.

findings.title: dueAt is a bare string compared numerically by isDue and lexically by repo.listDue, and nothing cross-checks them
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.dueAt` is typed `string` (`types.ts:92`) with the invariant "canonical ISO-8601 UTC timestamp" living only in comments. Two consumers read it with different orderings:
- `srs.ts:58` — `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()` (numeric, tolerant of any parseable format, yields `NaN` for garbage)
- `repo.ts:88` — `card.dueAt <= cutoff` (lexicographic string compare, correct only for zero-padded, same-offset ISO strings)

The `isDue` block in this file (lines 97-108) only ever feeds `dueAt` values it produced itself via `newCard`/`scheduleCard` or hand-wrote in canonical form. `repo.listDue` has no test at all (see L13-F13). So nothing anywhere pins the two comparisons to the same semantics. A non-padded `'2026-8-12'` is due under `isDue` and not due under `listDue`; `NaN` from an unparseable value makes `isDue` return `false` forever, so the card silently never surfaces again — a card that disappears rather than errors.

The type is the problem: `dueAt: string` lets any string in, and `ease`/`intervalDays` as bare `number`s are the same shape of footgun (`scheduleCard(card, grade)` is safe only because `Grade = 1|2|3|4` is a literal union — that part is done right). A branded `IsoTimestamp` produced by a single helper would make the two comparison sites provably consistent.

Verified sound in this file: `card(overrides)` on lines 7-22 builds from the real `newCard` factory and is annotated `: ReviewCard`, so the compiler enforces completeness — this is the honest-fixture pattern the rest of the suite should copy.

findings.title: coverForIsbn is tested with one perfect ISBN and undefined, so unvalidated ISBN text becomes Book.coverImageUrl
findings.description:
The `coverForIsbn` block has exactly two cases: a clean 13-digit ISBN and `undefined`. `GoodreadsRow.isbn13?: string` is unvalidated free text — `cleanIsbn` at `goodreads.ts:69-72` only strips the Goodreads `="..."` wrapper and returns whatever remains if it is non-empty. `coverForIsbn` then interpolates that directly into a URL and its `string | undefined` return type says nothing about whether the URL resolves.

`useLibrary.tsx:158` writes the result into a `Book`: `coverImageUrl: coverForIsbn(row.isbn13) ?? placeholderCover(row.title)`. Because a bad ISBN still yields a truthy string, the `??` placeholder fallback is bypassed and the book is persisted with a permanently-broken cover URL. Real Goodreads exports produce exactly the inputs no fixture covers: hyphenated ISBNs (`="978-0-7352-1129-2"` -> `covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/978-0-7352-1129-2-L.jpg`), 10-digit ISBNs, and placeholder values such as `="0"`. `Book.coverImageUrl: string` claims a usable image URL and delivers an arbitrary string.

What goes untested: every non-canonical ISBN shape, and the interaction that decides whether a Goodreads-imported book gets a real cover or a dead link.

Verified sound in the rest of this file: the `parseGoodreadsCsv` block (lines 10-93) is the strongest suite in the lot — it covers quoted commas, doubled quotes, embedded newlines, CRLF, column reordering, a missing optional column, and the skipped counter. The only gap there is that a blank interior line also increments `skipped` (parseCsv emits a `['']` row, whose empty title takes the skip branch at `goodreads.ts:99-102`), inflating the count shown to the user.
